question.text: The last sovereign emperor of the Inca was this son of Huayna Capac. who was strangled to death after providing the conquistador Francisco Pizarro with a room filled once with gold and twice with silver.
question.clue: He offered to fill a large room with gold and silver for his ransom, but the Spaniards didn't release him.

swap.leadin: Answer these questions about the native peoples of the Americas.
swap.text: This civilization, with capital at Cuzco and another city at Macchu Picchu, was conquered by Francisco Pizarro.
swap.clue: Descendants of this empire's royalty included Garcilaso de la Vega, and this empire was sometimes named for the four administrative suyus that it was divided into.

question.leadin: Answer the following about indigenous peoples of South America.
question.text: The Quechua group, who share their name with the language of the Inca Empire, live in and around this mountain range in Peru, Ecuador, and Bolivia.
question.clue: A culture in this mountain range depicted a spider called the "Decapitator" and created a mummy known as the Lord of Sipan.

swap.leadin: Answer these questions about Spanish conquistadores.
swap.text: This figure defeated a much larger force than his own at the battle of Cajamarca before conquering the Inca empire in 1532.
swap.clue: Gonzalo also led a revolt against Blasco Nunez Vela for attempting to enforce the New Laws under Charles V. Another man with this surname served under Balboa and briefly served as mayor of Panama City.

question.leadin: The "trophy heads" collected by this culture featured a hole in the skull where a rope was threaded through.
question.text: Name this culture who created geoglyphs in the shape of condors and hummingbirds in the desert, known as their namesake "lines."
question.clue: This culture built the Cantalloc ("cahn-TAH-yoke")Aqueducts, exemplifying the corkscrew entrances of their puquios ("poo-KEE-ohʼs").

swap.text: Paul Kosok discovered the Hummingbird, an earthwork built by these people indigenous to Peru. These people built the city of Cahuachi [ca-WA-chee] and used puquios to irrigate their crops.
swap.clue: Paul Kosok and Maria Reiche (RAI-keh) mapped structures created by these people.

question.leadin: This country is home to a Maoist cell called Shining Path, whose crackdown led to many human rights abuses by its ethnically Japanese president Alberto Fujimori in the 90s.
question.text: Name this country whose navy was beaten by nearby Chile in the War of the Pacific. This country just got back a trove of artifacts that Yale stole from Machu Picchu.
question.clue: A culture from this country based in Sipan was known for pottery depicting exaggerated sexual acts, and another civilization in this country was known for geoglyphs depicting Condors and Herons.

swap.text: Cusco was the capital of this South American empire.
swap.clue: This empire's language was Quechua, and these people built Machu Picchu.

question.leadin: Answer the following about a certain precious metal in pre-Columbian South America.
question.text: One of the leaders of this confederation ritually covered himself in gold dust before diving into Lake Guatavita. This confederation, which was led by a Zipa and a Zaque ["ZAH-kay"], held territory in the highlands of modern-day Colombia.
question.clue: Perhaps this polity's most well-known artefact is known as this polity's "raft", which is a gold sculpture that was found in Lake Guatavita.

swap.leadin: Answer these questions about pivotal ships from world history.
swap.text: This ship participated in most major engagements in Peruvian history during the latter half of the nineteenth century. It was named for the brother of Incan ruler Atahualpa.
swap.clue: This Peruvian ship sank the Esmeralda before Chile captured it in the War of the Pacific. It took its name from an Incan noble who lost a civil war to his brother Atahualpa.

question.leadin: The Aschers did work uncoding the number system used on these devices, where zero is represented by a missing knot.
question.text: Name these devices. Made from knotted string, these devices were extensively used in the administration of the Inca prior to their invasion by Francisco Pizarro.
question.clue: This objects that were used for record-keeping and other purposes by the Inca.

swap.leadin: As this man died, he drew a cross in his own blood.
swap.text: Name this man, the arch-rival of Diego Almagro. Before being killed by supporters of Almagro's son, he won the lopsided Battle of Cajamarca.
swap.clue: This man received help from longtime partner Diego Almagro, but he was killed by Almagro's forces in the Battle of Las Salinas.

question.text: Vilcabamba was founded by this Incan monarch. This monarch was captured by Spanish forces and imprisoned by the brothers of Francisco Pizarro before escaping and laying siege to Cusco for 10 months.

swap.leadin: Part of these people's confederation was ruled by a zipa, who would cover his body in gold dust and jump into Lake Guatavita along with some gold offerings.
swap.text: Name these people, whose confederation was ruled by a zipa in the south and a zaque in the north. The last powerful cacique of these people, Tundama, was killed with a large hammer by Balthasar Maldonado.
swap.clue: This confederation of Northern Andean tribes that was led by co-rulers called Zipa and Zaque. They were encountered by the Conquistador Gonzalo Jimenez de Quesada after his expedition sailed up the Magdalena.

question.leadin: According to one crackpot theory, these structures were built using medieval hot-air balloons.
question.text: Name these massive desert drawings that have been hypothesized to represent constellations. Greenpeace activists managed to damage one shaped like a hummingbird in late 2014.
question.answerHtml: Nazca Lines [accept Lines and Geoglyphs of Nasca and Palpa, accept Lineas de Nazca]
question.clue: These things were damaged by Greenpeace activists wearing improper footwear as part of a 2014 protest.

swap.leadin: Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa says that this man advised his son to not let anyone who raised two eyes against him live and gives his lifetime as an unrealistically long 125 years.
swap.text: Name this ruler, who reorganized his empire into the Tawantinsuyu, or "Land of the Four Corners."
swap.clue: This ruler, who legendarily subjugated the (+) Chanka people with stone warriors, organized his realm into four suyus.

question.text: The original "Maritime Foundations" theory was developed after the excavation of this site at the mouth of the Supe River that likely provided fish to Caral from the nearby ocean. This place is the type site of the Norte Chico.

swap.text: Lying at the confluence of the Huatanay and Tullmayo rivers, it was purportedly founded by Manco Capac. Among its tourist attractions is the church of La Merced.
swap.clue: This city whose Quechua name means "center."

question.leadin: The Met holds a work made of this material with French lettering and scenes from Greek mythology, and a lliklla ("LEEK-l'yah") made of this material that imitates Spanish-style lattice motifs.
question.text: Name this material used to make low-quality awasqa or high-quality qunpi ("COMB-pee"), decorated with tukapu motifs. A red llawt'u ("l'YAO-too") decorated the maskhaypacha, an imperial symbol made of this material.
question.answerHtml: camelid wool [or millma or millwa or willma; accept camelid hair or camelid fur; accept fleece in place of “wool”; accept llama, alpaca, or vicuña in place of “camelid”; prompt on hair or fur; prompt on textile or fabric or clothing or p’achakuna by asking “made of what substance?”; prompt on cotton or utkhu by asking “what material is more commonly used?”; reject “rope” or “chord”]

swap.leadin: Andy Watkins is a peasant in the Incan empire. Name some stuff about Andy's life.
swap.text: Andy is in Chan Chan and wants to tell his friends in Panchacamac about how much he loves e.e. cummings. He will have to solicit a chasqui messenger along the extensive Incan road system, who will store the information on one of these braided "talking knots."
swap.clue: Evidence for a writing system in these objects include a three-number sequence possibly representing the village of Puruchuco (poo-roo-CHOO-koh).
